Welcome to the Grimp Polar Viewer.
It lets you explore the Greenland Ice Sheet Mapping Project's velocity and radar products right in your web browser, on maps centered on the pole, the way polar scientists draw them.
Start by choosing a collection: annual, quarterly, monthly, or six- and twelve-day velocity, radar backscatter, or Terra SAR X glacier sites.
When you switch collections, the map stays where you are, so it's easy to compare data sets at one glacier.

Speed opens on a log scale, in the same colors as the Grimp browse images, so slow ice and fast glaciers like Jakobshavn both show. Untick log scale for a linear scale, then type a maximum or drag the clip slider to set its range.
The bar on the left is a timeline, newest at the top.
Drag the handles to set a range of dates, or click a tick to show that date.
Move the mouse over the map to read off the speed and its error.
To see how the ice has changed, open Time series at points and click a few spots.
Each one is read from every date and plotted as the values arrive.
The seasonal view shows the average for each month, with any one year drawn on top, so you can see the summer speed-up at a glance.

Tick Trend to fit each series: a straight line, or for monthly data, a line plus an annual cycle. The box gives the rate of change with its error, r squared and p, and the size and timing of the summer peak.
Plots can be saved as a picture, and the values as a CSV file.
For a profile, draw a line, or click Flow line and pick a point on a glacier.

The viewer traces the line along the ice flow. Drag the point to nudge it until the line follows the glacier the way you want, then click Use this line. A time axis along the top of the plot shows how many years the ice takes to travel down it.
Drag the slider under the buttons to make the line longer or shorter, upstream or downstream.
Each product you've shown gets its own curve, so you can see how the speed along the glacier has changed.
Click a date in the legend to hide its curve, or click its cross to remove it.
Set Plot to change from a date, and each curve shows how much faster or slower the ice is than it was then, all along the glacier.
You can add glacier names, calving fronts, basins and speed contours.
And you can turn on flow particles, which drift with the ice, to give a feel for how the whole system moves.
Strain rates shows how fast the ice is stretching, squeezing or shearing, worked out from the speed in the view.
Pick effective, along flow, shear or divergence, and how far apart to take the differences, then click Compute. Move the mouse over the map to read the value.
To watch change over time, open Animate and draw a box around a glacier.
Tick Anomaly and load the frames to see each year's difference from the average: red where the ice was faster than usual, blue where it was slower.
Save movie writes an M P 4 that plays in PowerPoint and on any computer.
Animations work for radar images too. Here, six years of backscatter show Jakobshavn's calving front moving back and forth with the seasons.
Swipe works on radar images too: a winter image on the left against late summer on the right shows how far the front moves in a few months.
Share this view copies a link that reopens exactly what you see, and the Q R code is handy for a poster or slide.
Embed copies code that puts this map, live, in your own web page.
Go to a glacier jumps straight to well known places, like Helheim.
Measure gives true distances and areas, corrected for the map projection. Drag a point to move it, or drag a side to add one.
Digitize draws your own points, lines, rectangles, circles and polygons, or freehand outlines traced with the mouse.
Drag inside a shape to move it, and drag a circle's edge to make it bigger or smaller.
Click plot beside a polygon to add it to Time series at points, as the average speed inside the shape on every date.

Type a name for each one in the list, then save them all as a Geo Package under a file name you choose, ready for Q G I S or Arc G I S. Open Geo Package brings shapes from those programs back in to edit, with all their fields.
In the Download section you can save Grimp products, or crop them to a box.
Other data drawn on the map, like glacier fronts, and the U C I basins and grounding lines, are for display only; their sources and credits, with download links, are on the GitHub page.
For many files, save a download list and fetch them with the command-line tool from the GitHub page.
And Open a folder reads a catalog and its Geo TIFFs from your own computer, so you can look at your own data without uploading anything.
Click Southern for Antarctica, and pick the Amundsen Sea velocity series to look at Pine Island Glacier.
Here the map shows the browse image, a shaded picture of the speed, but points and profiles still read the speed itself, so this point on the ice shelf plots how fast it has moved each year.
To compare two dates directly, turn on swipe and drag the handle across the glacier.
There's also a radar backscatter series for the Amundsen Sea, and a Nye-sar radar mosaic of the whole continent.
The full guide is on the GitHub page. Enjoy exploring.
